API reference / @jsprismarine/prismarine

@jsprismarine/prismarine ​

@jsprismarine/prismarine is the main package of the Prismarine project containing the core (& game logic) implementation of the server.

Prerequisites ​

Before you begin, ensure you have met the following requirements:

  • You have installed the latest version of Node.js and a package manager like npm, pnpm or bun.

Installation ​

To install @jsprismarine/prismarine, use the following command:

pnpm install @jsprismarine/prismarine --save

Worlds and dimensions ​

Each worlds.<name> entry in config.json is a Level: one save with one seed, clock, set of game rules and weather, and one World per dimension. The dimensions come from a Java worldgen/world_preset named by preset, with per-dimension overrides under dimensions. A stem's generator is built by the GeneratorFactories registry, whose built-in kinds are minecraft:noise, minecraft:flat, jsprismarine:void and minecraft:debug; register a { kind, build(context) } factory to add one. Portal travel between a level's worlds is the DimensionTravel service, reached through Server.getDimensionTravel(), with the cancelable entityPortalEnter and playerChangeDimension events. The guide is docs/data-driven/dimensions.md.

Inbound packet traces ​

Import InboundPacketTrace from @jsprismarine/prismarine/network/InboundPacketTrace and pass an instance as inboundPacketRecorder to the Server constructor. It captures accepted client packets with their process-local connection id, server-wide acceptance order, per-connection sequence, arrival tick, protocol version, and encoded bytes. Replay records across connections in the order returned by records(), awaiting each replayInboundRecord() call before the next. serialize() writes a versioned JSON trace, and InboundPacketTrace.deserialize() reads it back, including traces in the previous format version. The packet trace is separate from the initial-state manifest. Level.captureReplayInitialState() saves ready worlds, fails if a player or chunk write fails, and then records effective content and world-generation fingerprints, serializable RNG state, loaded-world digests, and a provider snapshot of persisted data. The built-in LevelDB provider captures every database record, level.dat, level.dat_old, levelname.txt, and fallback player-data JSON, including persisted chunks that were unloaded. Restore it with restoreReplayInitialStateSnapshot(provider, manifest) into a newly constructed, disabled provider before enabling it. Once the level has loaded the snapshot, call Level.restoreReplayRandomState(manifest) to verify level metadata and loaded-world digests, then restore RNG state. The manifest validates the snapshot digest, and providers without snapshot support reject capture and restore. LevelDB replaces records in one database batch, then restores metadata and player files, so restore is not atomic; discard the target if a file operation fails after the database write. The provider snapshot covers persisted data, but not runtime state or pending simulation work, and does not fingerprint executable server or plugin code. Capturing also fails when the server uses a custom random callback without a serializable state contract. A NetworkDispatcher can feed each record back through its decoded handler path; the built-in server exposes that method through server.getKernel().get(networkToken).replayInboundRecord?.(record, tickOffset). The caller must restore matching connections and advance the server to each recorded tick. Pass an OutboundPacketTrace as outboundPacketRecorder to the Server constructor to capture encoded clientbound packets and compare their per-tick digests. World.replayStateDigest() hashes loaded chunks, pending chunk load coordinates and priorities, block update positions and due ticks, scheduled block and fluid ticks, the Java random tick generator state, light queue depth, entities, level weather and rules, and player inventories. Scheduler entries retain their trigger time, priority, and insertion order. Light work is represented by queue depth to keep each digest bounded, so the digest does not identify queued light nodes. These digest fields detect divergence but do not restore pending work or the per-world random tick generator. It also does not cover unloaded chunks or every pending simulation subsystem.

packages/client/src/SessionReplay.test.ts exercises the live replay path with two flat replay worlds using seed 2847. It captures a provider snapshot before client login, restores that snapshot into both replay worlds, then replays four scripted MovePlayerPacket records from a real client through networkToken. The test logs the same two identities into each world and compares world and outbound packet digests at each tick. It seeds Server randomness, fixes the remaining global random calls, and disables natural mob spawning in the flat fixture so unrelated spawn timing does not change the world digest. Login remains live because the trace does not restore connection lifecycle or pre-login sessions; the test maps the captured connection order and input entity id onto each live session. Its per-tick outbound digest normalizes process-local actor ids by the logged-in players and by first-seen packet order for other actors before hashing packet bytes. The test does not cover frame grouping, restoration of in-memory runtime or pending simulation state, complete lighting work queues, or Java-verified entity update order. Packet bytes and snapshots may include player data, so keep capture opt-in and protect any trace or manifest you store. The packet benchmark measures dispatcher recording and replay CPU plus serialized packet-trace storage, but it does not measure world ticks or digests.

The performance-tagged case in packages/client/src/SessionReplay.test.ts replays the same fixed movement trace with packet recording and per-tick digests disabled, then enabled. Both runs log in first; the baseline installs no packet recorders and maps the mover from its captured connection id, since the mover connects first in both runs. It reports tick CPU and wall time, per-tick world and outbound digest CPU, checkpoint snapshot capture, manifest validation and RNG-restore cost, and trace and manifest sizes. Manifest size includes the provider snapshot. Snapshot restore runs during world setup outside this measurement. Outbound trace size is a JSON record estimate, not a measurement of its in-memory JavaScript objects. Run pnpm --filter @jsprismarine/client exec vitest run --config vitest.config.ts src/SessionReplay.test.ts to run the live replay test, or add -t "reports replay instrumentation cost against an unrecorded baseline" to that command to run the performance measurement. Run pnpm --filter @jsprismarine/prismarine run bench:inbound-packets to reproduce the packet-only benchmark.

JSON Schemas ​

The server uses config.json for its settings.

Draft 7 schemas for the package's JSON configuration and data files are included in the published package under schemas/. JSON object files receive a $schema URL for the build that last wrote them. Package builds and release executables use their exact version. Standalone nightly executables use the unstable npm dist-tag, which resolves to the latest unstable package. The files ops.json and banned-players.json contain arrays at the root and carry their schema URL in a leading comment. These URLs use UNPKG, so standalone server users do not need to install an npm package to access the schemas.

Block.getJavaTags() and Item.getJavaTags() expose Java datapack tag membership after the content stack loads. hasJavaTag(name) checks one membership. Their getTags() and hasTag(name) methods continue to expose Bedrock tags.

Startup benchmark ​

bench:startup compares source and built server startup with Node's compile cache disabled, cold, and warm. Each run starts from a fresh temporary JSP_DIR with the same flat-world configuration and seed. The report includes time and main-thread CPU until the server listens, heap use, and the content-build, command-build, and world-manager-enable phases.

sh
pnpm --filter @jsprismarine/prismarine run bench:startup
pnpm --filter @jsprismarine/prismarine run bench:trends -- --scenarios startup --write /tmp/startup-baseline.json

Block-state allocation benchmark ​

bench:block-state-allocation measures retained heap after buildServerContent() and CPU time inside resolveBlocks() with the default vanilla stack. The benchmark notes record the baseline comparison, current PR head measurements, and commands for reproducing both.

Content snapshot benchmark ​

pnpm run bench:content-snapshot compares fresh content builds with a V8 startup snapshot. The snapshot keeps resolved seed-independent registries and a rebindable world source; each restored process redirects captured world views to its own adapter and rebuilds seed-bound Java and Bedrock loot streams. The benchmark checks content digests and registry identity across seeds, and reports custom-pack invalidation. Pass -- --vanilla to use the fetched default pack stack instead of the small fixture.

Terrain proto cache ​

Callers that construct DataDrivenGenerator can opt into a bounded disk cache for immutable terrain status tiles with persistentProtoCache. The default stays off. Records are keyed by the seed, dimension, worldgen settings, effective datapack registries, template contents, generator version, cache schema, and chunk position. A corrupt or incompatible record is removed, then the generator rebuilds that terrain tile. Choose a dedicated directory and a byte limit for it.

ts
const generator = new DataDrivenGenerator({
    registries,
    templates,
    persistentProtoCache: {
        directory: join(worldDirectory, 'terrain-proto-cache'),
        maxBytes: 512 * 1024 * 1024
    }
});

Custom template sources need a stable worldgenFingerprint for the cache to start. Custom structure builders and worker pipelines are not supported with persistent terrain caching. Run pnpm --filter @jsprismarine/prismarine run bench:terrain-cache to compare an 11 by 11 preload and a 3 by 3 player return after six distant chunk requests. The benchmark reports cache storage, record bytes written, write amplification, and time saved against regeneration.

Shared terrain tiles ​

Worker-based whole-chunk generation can also share a bounded in-memory store for immutable terrain tiles. It is opt-in and lasts only as long as the generator's process. When every slot is occupied, or a tile is larger than maxTileBytes, the worker builds that tile locally. A worker exit releases any unpublished claims from that worker; completed tiles remain available to the other workers.

ts
import { DataDrivenGenerator, defaultChunkPipeline } from '@jsprismarine/prismarine/world/generators/datadriven/DataDrivenGenerator';
import { SharedTerrainTileStore } from '@jsprismarine/prismarine/world/generators/datadriven/SharedTerrainTileStore';

const terrainTiles = new SharedTerrainTileStore({
    maxBytes: 32 * 1024 * 1024,
    maxTileBytes: 512 * 1024
});
const generator = new DataDrivenGenerator({
    registries,
    sharedTerrainTileStore: terrainTiles,
    chunks: { pipeline: defaultChunkPipeline(), workers: 4 }
});

The complete seed, dimension, generator settings, effective registry and template fingerprints, generation flags, and chunk coordinates identify each tile. Custom template sources need a stable worldgenFingerprint. Run pnpm --filter @jsprismarine/prismarine run bench:chunks with the chunks arm and the shared tile-store mode to compare throughput and memory with worker-local generation.

Enumerations ​

DamageCause ​

Defined in: prismarine/src/entity/DamageCause.ts:10

What hurt an entity. Carried through so a death can be reported as what it was, and so the things that ignore particular kinds of damage have something to test.

Its own file rather than a member of Entity, because DamageSource has to name both this and Entity, and Entity has to name DamageSource - which is the runtime cycle the import rules in biome.json exist to prevent. Entity re-exports it, so the older import { DamageCause } from './entity/Entity' still resolves and nothing had to be rewritten.

What a break knows about itself, beyond the block that broke.

Properties ​

blockEntity? ​

readonly optional blockEntity?: BlockEntityData

Defined in: prismarine/src/block/blockLoot.ts:198

What the block was holding, read before the break took it.

Java's LootContextParams.BLOCK_ENTITY, which the shulker box table's copy_components reads: its minecraft:container is what the dropped box carries away. A bed's or banner's color is read from it too, to pick the table of the right color. Left out for a block that holds nothing, which is every block whose table never looks.

explosionRadius? ​

readonly optional explosionRadius?: number

Defined in: prismarine/src/block/blockLoot.ts:187

The radius of the blast that broke it, for a block an explosion took out.

Java's LootContextParams.EXPLOSION_RADIUS, which every vanilla block table reads through its minecraft:explosion_decay function: each item in a rolled stack survives with a chance of 1 / radius, so a stone blown up by TNT yields cobblestone three times in four and nothing the fourth. Left out for an ordinary break, which keeps every item.

CommandExecutor ​

Defined in: prismarine/src/command/CommandExecutor.ts:13

Something that can issue a command and be answered.

A player and the server console have exactly this much in common: a name and somewhere to put a reply. They are not the same kind of thing otherwise - one stands at a position in a world and the other is a terminal attached to the process - so this is an interface rather than a shared base class. Making the console an entity to get these four methods is what forced isPlayer() and isConsole() to exist in the first place.

ConfigDocument ​

Defined in: prismarine/src/config/ConfigDocument.ts:26

A config file held as text, edited one path at a time.

Reading parses the text; writing changes only the part of the text the path names, so a comment or a blank line a person put in the file stays where it was. Replacing a value replaces everything under it, including comments inside a replaced list or map, since there is nothing to attach them to afterwards.

destroy()? ​

optional destroy(at, options?): boolean

Defined in: prismarine/src/content/world/adapter.ts:125

Takes a block out: raises its onBreak and puts what Java's table rolls on the ground.

The write is still the caller's and has to come afterwards, because a family reads the block entity it is about to lose. src/world/blockDestroy.ts is the one place that knows how, and this is how a content package reaches it: a piston popping a torch and a falling anvil clearing a flower both go through here rather than guessing that a block drops one of itself.

Left out by an adapter with no live world behind it, which sends the caller back to the drop it would have made on its own.

ContentPosition

options? ​

Properties ​

biomeSource? ​

readonly optional biomeSource?: BiomeSourceDefinition

Defined in: prismarine/src/world/generators/datadriven/DataDrivenGenerator.ts:178

The biome layout of the default key, as the biome_source of a level stem describes it.

A definition rather than a built BiomeSource, because the worker threads build their own generator and an object with closures cannot cross a thread. A multi_noise preset resolves through the reports/biome_parameters registry. Defaults to the minecraft:overworld preset.

carve? ​

Defined in: prismarine/src/world/generators/datadriven/DataDrivenGenerator.ts:182

chunks? ​

readonly optional chunks?: ChunkPoolOptions

Defined in: prismarine/src/world/generators/datadriven/DataDrivenGenerator.ts:259

Where to run whole chunks, and how many at a time.

Absent by default, which builds them on this thread. This is the pool that pays: a terrain pool leaves the decoration pass and the structure layout here, which is 168 of the 239 milliseconds a chunk costs, so no worker count takes it past 1.33 times. A pool of whole chunks makes all but the Bedrock translation parallel.

Pool options are alternatives, not layers. DataDrivenGeneratorOptions.stages takes precedence when supplied; otherwise this option takes precedence over DataDrivenGeneratorOptions.terrain, because a worker running the whole ladder runs its own terrain inside it.

terrain? ​

readonly optional terrain?: TerrainPoolOptions

Defined in: prismarine/src/world/generators/datadriven/DataDrivenGenerator.ts:235

Where to run the terrain bodies, and how many at a time.

Absent by default, which runs them on this thread. A pool is worth about 4.7 times one thread at five or six workers on an Apple M1 Pro, and less past that, because six of its eight cores are performance cores and a worker is a whole V8 isolate.

Only terrain goes to a worker. It writes radius 0, its own chunk and nothing else, so two of them can never touch the same block. Use DataDrivenGeneratorOptions.stages to move features as well.

DimensionType ​

Defined in: prismarine/src/world/DimensionType.ts:33

How tall a dimension is, where its floor sits, and what the client and the save call it.

Every vertical bound in the chunk stack derives from one of these rather than from a constant, because the three vanilla dimensions do not agree on any of them: the Overworld starts at -64 and is 384 blocks tall, the Nether starts at 0 and is 128 as far as the client is concerned, the End starts at 0 and is 256.

The sub chunk index is the y coordinate shifted right by four, and stays signed: index -4 is the Overworld's bottom sub chunk, covering y -64 to -49. That is also exactly how the index byte is stored in a Bedrock world's sub chunk records, so nothing needs rebasing on the way to disk.

EntitySpawn ​

Defined in: prismarine/src/world/EntitySpawn.ts:12

A mob world generation decided should exist, recorded rather than created.

The generator builds chunks and knows nothing about the world they will belong to - it has no entity list to add to, and a chunk may well be generated long before anything asks for it. So a pass that builds a village says "a villager belongs here" and the world creates it when the chunk is first loaded.

Deliberately data rather than an Entity: an entity needs a Position, a position needs a world, and a world is exactly what the generator does not have.

locate()? ​

optional locate(request): StructureSearchResult | undefined

Defined in: prismarine/src/world/Generator.ts:238

The nearest structure a search accepts, without generating anything.

This is what /locate asks. A structure's position is a function of the seed and the placement grid alone, so the answer comes from laying candidates out against the bare noise terrain: no chunk is built, nothing is written, and a search over thousands of blocks costs a few hundred layout attempts rather than thousands of chunks.

Synchronous, like Generator.surfaceAt and for the same reason: the command layer that asks is synchronous, and the work is arithmetic rather than a chunk.

Optional, because a generator that places no structures has nothing to find.

raiseUrgency()? ​

optional raiseUrgency(cx, cz, urgency): void

Defined in: prismarine/src/world/Generator.ts:210

Says that a chunk already asked for is wanted more than it was.

A chunk is requested once and waited on by everybody who wants it, so the band it was given is whoever asked first. A rim chunk queued as idle is the chunk a player is standing on a moment later, and nothing else would move it up.

Only affects a request still waiting for a worker. One already being built finishes at the speed it was going to finish at either way.

Optional, because a generator with no queue has no turn to move.

number

Chunk x of the request.

cz ​

number

"idle" | "immediate" | "soon"

stopGenerating()? ​

optional stopGenerating(): void

Defined in: prismarine/src/world/Generator.ts:301

Gives up every chunk request that has not started yet, for a server that is shutting down.

A generator that answers one request at a time holds a queue, and a start region fills that queue thirty-two chunks at a time. Waiting for it to drain means a shutdown spends seconds generating terrain that the save it is about to run will not even look at. The request that is already running finishes, so no half-generated chunk is handed back; everything behind it rejects with GenerationStopped.

Optional, because a generator that answers immediately has no queue to give up.

Returns ​

void

optional structureSpawnOverrideAt(identifier, at, seed?): boolean | undefined

Generators without Java structure data omit the query. A generator with Java data returns undefined for an entity that also appears in Java's biome spawn tables or has no structure override. Structure-only entities return false outside matching overrides and true inside one.

surfaceAt()? ​

optional surfaceAt(x, z, seed?): SurfaceProbe

Defined in: prismarine/src/world/Generator.ts:177

The topmost block of one column, without generating the chunk it is in.

The answer comes from the bare terrain: no surface rule has run and nothing has decorated, so a flooded column reads as water and a wooded one reads as the ground under the trees rather than as a canopy. That is Java's ChunkGenerator.getBaseHeight, and it is what a spawn search wants - whether a player can stand here is a question about the land, and answering it by generating a finished chunk costs four orders of magnitude more.

Optional, because a generator with no cheaper answer than its own chunks has nothing to add here and a caller falls back to generating one.

Defined in: prismarine/src/config/JsonConfigTypes.ts:77

The world seed, read the way Java reads the text in its world creation box: a value that parses as a 64-bit integer is that integer, and anything else is its String.hashCode.

Spell it as a string. A Java seed is a 64-bit integer and a JSON or YAML number is a double, which is exact only below 2^53. Written as a number, 8475011743740320021 is read back as 8475011743740319744 and generates a different world. A number is still accepted for configs written before this, and is exact for seeds below 2^53.

bedrockPacks? ​

readonly optional bedrockPacks?: readonly string[] | "all"

Defined in: prismarine/src/content/packStack.ts:56

Which packs to compose out of a BDS behavior_packs folder, by header UUID, or 'all' for every pack the folder holds.

Defaults to the vanilla behavior pack alone. BDS ships chemistry, the editor, the server script libraries and four experimental toggles in that folder, and a world composes those only when it turns them on; a server aiming at vanilla parity turns none of them on. Education Edition content is out of scope by plan section 12 decision 8, and the editor's five editor: entities are tools for a world author rather than content a server serves.

The packs are on disk either way, so naming one here is how a server that does want it opts in.

PipelineKey ​

Defined in: prismarine/src/world/generators/datadriven/DataDrivenGenerator.ts:443

What picks one compiled pipeline out of a generator shared between dimensions: the settings a level stem names and the dimension it fills. The seed is the other half of the cache key and travels separately, because one key serves every world on the server that uses that stem.

Plain data, because every task carries its key across the worker boundary and the worker compiles the pipeline from it. One generator and one worker pool therefore serve the Overworld, the Nether and the End instead of three of each.

Defined in: prismarine/src/config/JsonConfigTypes.ts:345

The Java id of the dimension the player was in, such as minecraft:the_nether.

The LevelDB provider also writes it as Bedrock's DimensionId integer. Absent on a record written before this field existed, which reads as the Overworld.

Java drives all three rows of an enchanting table from one generator seeded with this, which is what keeps the rows still while a player puts an item in and takes it out again. Kept across a login for the same reason: a table that redrew on every join would be a different table.

ParseTargetSelector() ​

ParseTargetSelector(__namedParameters): Entity[]

Defined in: prismarine/src/utils/ParseTargetSelector.ts:31

Parse target selector argument.

Parameters ​

__namedParameters ​
entities ​

Entity[]

input ​

string

random? ​

() => number = Math.random

Random draw for @r, supplied by the live server during command execution.

source ​

Entity

Returns ​

Entity[]

The entities matching the target query

Remarks ​

A target selector is made up of 3 parts:

  • First there's the @ (at symbol) part, notifying us that this is in fact a target selector

  • Secondly there's the target selector type (a, e, p, r, s), this specifies what kind of entities we should query for and in what way.

  • Thirdly there's the arguments, they are split up in a comma-separated list in the argument=value format.

This results in an input similar to: @e[type=player,gamemode=creative,limit=3]

Builds every content registry from a pack stack.

The order is forced by what each step needs. The behavior families are registered before their domain resolves, because resolution attaches them; the item factory is deferred and bound afterwards, because the families are registered before the item registry they build stacks from exists; and the goals are registered before the reference entity components, because the component registration skips names that are already taken and the goals are the implementations the server wants.

checkIdentifiers() ​

checkIdentifiers(definitions, options?): Diagnostic[]

Defined in: prismarine/src/content/unmappedIdentifiers.ts:68

Resolves every Java identifier the loaded pack stack references and reports the ones nothing accounts for.

Non-strict is a report rather than a refusal, for the same reason the content build reports the defaults it had to invent instead of stopping: a server that would otherwise run should run, and the operator should be told exactly what will be missing. Each unaccounted identifier is one error-severity diagnostic naming the pack and the file, so the startup line that counts content errors counts these too. Strict turns the same list into UnmappedIdentifierError.

A reviewed loss is not reported. It is already written down, with a reason and a reference, in @jsprismarine/mapping's loss list, and the parity dashboard counts it from there.

contentRegistryIds() ​

contentRegistryIds(content): ContentRegistryIds

Defined in: prismarine/src/command/vanillaCommands.ts:57

The four registries whose contents a command argument validates against.

Mojang's published command enums are frozen at the version the table was generated from, so validating against them alone refuses a pack's own mypack:dragon at parse for an entity this server can spawn. These four are the registries a host verb resolves an id against and a pack can extend, so each is offered alongside Mojang's list rather than instead of it.

The registries left out fail that test for their own reasons. minecraft:mob_effect uses Mojang's published list because the host keeps no custom effect registry. minecraft:attribute, minecraft:particle_type and minecraft:worldgen/biome are not validated by anybody: Bedrock publishes no enum for them, so they already reach a command body as an unchecked string.

Parameters ​

content ​

ServerContent

The server's content build.

ContentRegistryIds

One id list per validated registry.

Builds the eight block adapter members over one dimension's storage.

set commits the write before it raises onPlace, because the hook is documented to run with the new state already readable, and notifies the neighbors afterwards so a behavior that writes its own state during onPlace has done so before anything reads it back.

A write that leaves the same block standing raises onBlockStateChange instead of onPlace, once per state value that moved. That is what the two hooks are documented to mean, and it is also what makes the write terminate: a door opens by rewriting its own open_bit, so onPlace would call the family that is calling it.

createNoiseGeneratorFactory() ​

createNoiseGeneratorFactory(): GeneratorFactory

Defined in: prismarine/src/world/generators/factories/noise.ts:48

A minecraft:noise factory whose stems share one DataDrivenGenerator.

The first stem built opens the generator from the context's registries, with a pool of worker threads sized by the context's workers or the core count. Every stem after that, the Nether's and the End's included, gets a view of the same generator keyed by its settings, its biome source and its dimension, so a server runs one pool of min(6, cores - 2) workers rather than one per dimension. The stem's settings names a worldgen/noise_settings document or carries one inline; the inline form travels under a private id. A host that cannot run workers generates on the server thread and says so once.

One factory per GeneratorFactories registry, which is one per server: the registry's stopGenerating reaches the shared generator through any of the views it built.

Returns ​

GeneratorFactory

Throws ​

When the Java data is not on disk, or the settings id is not a registered worldgen/noise_settings document, or the biome source cannot be built.

structureNameMatches() ​

structureNameMatches(name, structure): boolean

Defined in: prismarine/src/world/World.ts:166

Whether a structure identifier is what a player meant by a name.

Bedrock's /locate structure names a family - village, ruinedportal - where Java has one identifier per variant, so an exact comparison would find none of them. Three spellings are accepted, from most to least specific: the full identifier, the path on its own, and the path with a variant suffix, which is what makes village find minecraft:village_plains.

Underscores are dropped from the comparison so Bedrock's ruinedportal reaches Java's ruined_portal.

Parameters ​

name ​

string

What the player typed.

structure ​

string

A structure identifier the generator knows.

Returns ​

boolean

toPacketCompressionLevel() ​

toPacketCompressionLevel(raw): number

Defined in: prismarine/src/config/Config.ts:211

Clamps a configured zlib level to the range zlib accepts.

zlib takes -1 (its own default) through 9 and errors on anything else. The value comes straight out of a hand edited config file, and an unchecked 10 reached deflate as a rejection on the chunk sending path, which is nowhere near where the typo was, and used to take the server's tick down with it. Clamping keeps a bad number a bad number rather than an outage.

Parameters ​

raw ​

unknown

The value read from the config file, of whatever type the file held.

Returns ​

number

An integer from -1 to 9, or the default of 7 when raw is not an integer.

toPacketCompressionThreshold() ​

toPacketCompressionThreshold(raw): number

Defined in: prismarine/src/config/Config.ts:226

Bounds the configured threshold to a protocol-safe unsigned 16-bit value.

Zero disables compression, matching Bedrock's NetworkSettings semantics; positive values compress batch bodies at or above that size.

Parameters ​

raw ​

unknown

The value read from the config file, of whatever type the file held.

Returns ​

number

An integer from 0 to 65,535, or the default of 256 when raw is not an integer.
